title: DataFrames First: Load, Inspect, Slice
objective: After this lesson you will be able to load CSVs with explicit dtypes, profile them (shape, dtypes, nulls, describe), and slice with loc/iloc, boolean masks, and sorting — stating what each inspection is for.
why: Every analysis starts with first contact: what rows exist, what types parsed, what's missing. Skipping inspection means analyzing assumptions — string prices sorting lexicographically, dates as objects, silent NaNs. Profiling (shape/dtypes/nulls/describe) takes minutes and prevents hours of wrong-number debugging later.

blocks.text: `read_csv` infers types — and inference guesses wrong on messy files (IDs as ints dropping leading zeros, mixed columns as objects). Declare `dtype` for keys/IDs (strings, always), `parse_dates` for timestamps, `na_values` for the file's missing markers ('', 'N/A', '-'). Explicit loading converts surprises into declarations.

blocks.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO
csv = "order_id,customer,total,placed\nORD-1,Ana,129.00,2026-10-01\nORD-2,Ben,,2026-10-02\n"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv), dtype={"order_id": str}, parse_dates=["placed"])
print(df.dtypes.to_dict())
print("shape:", df.shape, "nulls:", int(df.isna().sum().sum()))

blocks.text: Four probes, every dataset, no exceptions: **shape** (row/column counts — sanity vs source claims), **dtypes** (parsed as intended?), **nulls** (`isna().sum()` per column — missingness map), **describe** (ranges/means that expose outliers: negative prices, future dates, 0-row tables). Profiling output belongs in the data dossier (OpenDataLoader thinking, pandas execution).

blocks.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO
csv = "item,price,qty\nRunner,129.00,2\nSandal,59.50,1\nRunner,129.00,1\n"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv))
print(df.describe().loc["mean"].to_dict())
print("dupes:", int(df.duplicated().sum()))
mask = (df["price"] > 100) & (df["qty"] >= 2)
print(df.loc[mask, ["item", "price"]].to_dict("records"))

blocks.text: Slice deliberately: loc, iloc, masks, sorting

**loc** (label-based, inclusive), **iloc** (positional), **boolean masks** (composable with &/|/~ and parentheses — `and`/`or` fail elementwise), **sort_values** (by columns, NaN placement stated). Chained assignment (`df[a][b] = x`) warns (SettingWithCopyWarning) — assign via single `.loc` to write what you mean.

blocks.title: Mask the rows
blocks.note: Run it: the boolean-mask + multi-key-sort logic twins of pandas filtering. Masks compose with AND/OR/NOT (parenthesized); sorts break ties explicitly — same discipline, both languages.

items: Declare dtypes/parse_dates/na_values on load — inference guesses, declarations hold
Profile always: shape, dtypes, nulls, describe — minutes that prevent hours
loc/iloc/masks/sorts with composable boolean logic; single-.loc assignment only

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice mask/sort twin and record outputs. (b) In Python (your env), load a 5-row CSV with one missing price and report shape/dtypes/nulls/means. (c) Select high-value multi-qty rows with a two-condition mask and state why parentheses are mandatory.
hints: Twin outputs: matching 1 (Runner), top Runner:2 (price tie broken by qty).
Profile lines: dtypes dict, null count, describe means — each answering what/which/how-much.
Parentheses: & / | bind tighter than comparisons in pandas — unparenthesized masks evaluate wrong (or raise); always wrap each condition.
exercise.why: Twin parity (JS logic mirrors pandas), profile completeness (four probes), and precedence discipline (parentheses mandatory) are the three first-contact judgments.

options: String dtype: lexicographic order — parse to numeric on load (dtype/converters), quarantine unparseable
quiz.explain: Inferred object dtype sorts textually ('9' > '80' lexicographically), so string prices order wrongly. Declare numeric dtypes (or converters) on load and quarantine the unparseable.

options: and/or don't elementwise — use & / | with parenthesized conditions per side
quiz.explain: Python and/or coerce whole Series truthiness (ambiguous → error). Elementwise &/| with parentheses per condition is the rule.

quiz.q: SettingWithCopyWarning on chained assignment. Meaning + fix?
options: Uncertain view-vs-copy: write may vanish — assign via single .loc[row_mask, col] instead
quiz.explain: Chained indexing may return views or copies unpredictably. Single .loc assignment writes deterministically.

summary: Declared dtypes, four-probe profiles, composable masks, explicit sorts, single-.loc writes. First contact done right prevents wrong-number archaeology.
